title: Locking
lead: Lock compatibility, two-phase locking, strict locking and deadlock handling.
goals: Strict locking and the source schedule

sections.title: Lock modes and compatibility
sections.html:
A lock manager grants access before operations execute. Shared (S) locks permit reads; exclusive (X) locks protect writes. Several transactions may hold S on the same object, but X conflicts with both S and X held by another transaction.

An incompatible request waits or triggers an abort according to the concurrency-control policy. The lock table records holders and waiting requests. Upgrading S to X must also satisfy compatibility.

Acquiring a lock for each operation is insufficient for serializability if a transaction releases a lock and later reacquires locks freely. A protocol must constrain the lifetime of those locks.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Two-phase locking
sections.html:
Two-phase locking (2PL) separates a transaction into a growing phase, in which it acquires or upgrades locks, and a shrinking phase, in which it releases locks. After its first release it cannot acquire a new lock or upgrade one.

2PL guarantees conflict serializability for the lock-protected objects, but admits only a subset of conflict-serializable schedules. It does not require knowing every future operation in advance.

Basic 2PL can release write locks before commit and allow another transaction to read uncommitted data, causing cascading aborts. It can also deadlock. These are distinct limitations addressed by stricter lock retention and deadlock handling.

PDF pp. 7–12

sections.title: Strict locking and the source schedule
sections.html:
The source’s strict-2PL presentation retains all locks until transaction completion. Terminology varies: retaining X locks to the end is often called strict 2PL, while retaining both S and X locks is also called rigorous 2PL.

Retaining write locks prevents other transactions from reading or overwriting uncommitted changes. On abort, restoring old values does not invalidate committed readers of those uncommitted values because such readers were blocked.

The source compares a transfer of 100 from A to B with a transaction summing both balances. Releasing and reacquiring locks without 2PL permits the incorrect total 1900. The controlled schedules return the consistent total 2000.

PDF pp. 13–17

sections.title: Deadlock detection
sections.html:
A deadlock occurs when transactions form a cycle of waiting for each other’s locks. It is represented by a waits-for graph: Tᵢ → Tⱼ means Tᵢ is waiting for a lock held by Tⱼ. This differs from the precedence graph used to test schedule serializability.

The DBMS periodically searches for cycles. To break one it aborts a victim and releases its locks. Victim choice can consider age, work performed, held locks and previous restarts; fairness policies reduce starvation.

Detection frequency trades checking overhead against waiting time. Conservative 2PL avoids deadlocks by acquiring all required locks before execution, at the cost of knowing them in advance and potentially reducing concurrency.

PDF pp. 18–22

sections.title: Wait-die and wound-wait
sections.html:
Assign each transaction a timestamp; older transactions have higher priority. In wait-die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester aborts when the holder is older.

In wound-wait, an older requester aborts a younger holder; a younger requester waits for an older holder. Only one age direction is allowed for waits in each scheme, so a waiting cycle cannot form.

Restarted transactions retain their original timestamp to avoid repeatedly losing priority. The rules refer specifically to requester and holder; reversing those roles reverses the decision.

PDF pp. 23–28

quiz.question: T_old requests a lock held by T_new. What does wound-wait do?
options: T_new aborts and releases its locks
quiz.explanation: Under wound-wait, a transaction with a smaller timestamp can force a younger transaction holding the requested lock to abort.

source.summary: Lecture 20 covers shared and exclusive locks, 2PL, strict 2PL, deadlock detection, and the wait-die and wound-wait prevention rules.
